title: The dorsal horn: first stop in the CNS
objective: Describe where sensory afferents terminate in the dorsal horn and why layering matters.

steps.title: Where the periphery meets the CNS
steps.body: A sensory [[afferent]]'s central branch enters the spinal cord and ends in the **[[dorsal horn]]**, which is organized in layers (**[[Rexed laminae]]**). Different afferents end at different depths: small [[nociceptor|nociceptors]] (C, Aδ) terminate superficially; large touch fibers (Aβ) dive to deeper laminae.

steps.prompt: Why does it matter that C fibers and Aβ fibers end in different dorsal-horn layers?
options: It keeps pain and touch information in partly separate circuits
It makes the C fibers conduct faster than the Aβ touch fibers do
It means touch and pain can never interact with each other at all
It decides which of the fibers are myelinated and which are not
steps.explanation: Laminar targeting sorts modalities into partly distinct circuits — the anatomical basis for processing pain and touch differently (and for them to interact, as in gate control).

variants.setup: C and Aβ fibers terminate at different depths in the dorsal horn.
variants.prompt: What does that layering buy the circuit?
options: Partly separate processing of pain vs touch
Faster conduction in the C fibers
A guarantee the two never interact
variants.reveal: Different target layers let pain and touch be processed partly separately — while still allowing defined interactions.

steps.prompt: Match each fiber to where it mainly terminates.
steps.explanation: Small nociceptive fibers end superficially; large low-threshold touch fibers end deeper — the layout that modality-specific circuits are built on.

steps.title: A relay, not a wire
steps.body: The dorsal horn isn't a passive junction. Local interneurons, descending inputs, and convergence all shape the signal here before it ascends. The next lessons follow what happens to it.

reviewNotes: Dorsal horn + laminar termination; sets up gate control and ascending paths.
